title: A Kingdom for Kumbhanda
subtitle: Aniruddha and Usha are wed as Bana's realm finds a new king
story:
The war for Aniruddha was over, and the victors were doing something unusual with the conquered city: they were turning the enemy king's palace into a wedding hall.

Krishna had come to Sonitpura to bring home his grandson, who had been carried off from Dwaraka in the night and bound in the women's quarters of the demon king Bana with nooses of living serpents. The campaign had ended strangely. Shiva himself had fought beside Bana and then withdrawn; Bana had been spared, honored with boons, and sent on his way in the company of the god who had blessed him. Only one thing still weighed on Krishna: the boy he had come to save. Again and again he asked the sage Narada where Aniruddha lay, his worry for the child growing with every answer, and each time the sage told him the same thing — that the prince was bound with serpent-nooses in the palace's inner apartments.

It was Chitralekha who opened the way: Usha's friend, the one whose cleverness had first brought the two young people together. Telling them plainly that this was the women's apartment of Bana, she led Krishna, Balarama, Pradyumna, Narada, and Garuda inside, and the rescue required no battle at all. At the sight of Garuda, the serpents clinging to Aniruddha's body in the shape of arrows released him at once and dropped to the floor as spent shafts. The prince, overjoyed, saluted Krishna, bowed to Balarama and to Garuda, and then approached his own father, Pradyumna. Beside him Usha, encircled by her friends, saluted Krishna and the great bird, and with shyness bowed to Pradyumna as well.

Narada, smiling, showered blessings on the reunion and hailed Krishna's good fortune at being united again with Pradyumna and Aniruddha. Then the sage made a request that drew laughter from all the Yadavas, as Krishna's clan was called: let the marriage that had been won by prowess be celebrated for Aniruddha, he said, for he had a great desire to hear the two families trade jokes, as a bridegroom's party and a bride's do at such times. Krishna answered that it would soon be accomplished.

At that moment Kumbhanda arrived, carrying all the articles for a wedding, and bowed before Krishna asking for safety. He was Bana's minister — the man who had counselled mercy toward Aniruddha during the war — and Narada had quietly asked Krishna to keep him from leaving. Krishna raised him up and promised him protection, saying he had been pleased by his good deeds. "You will now become the king of this kingdom," he told him. "I confer this kingdom on you. Live forever under my protection, happy and self-controlled, with all your kinsmen."

Then Krishna celebrated the wedding of Aniruddha, and the god of fire himself stood present among the guests. Aniruddha bathed and was adorned with ornaments; the Apsaras, the dancing maidens of heaven, cut jokes with him; the Gandharvas, heaven's singers, raised melodious, auspicious songs while the Apsaras danced, and the whole marriage party shone.

When the rites were done, Krishna honored Rudra, the god who grants boons, and made ready to depart for Dwaraka with the celestials. But Kumbhanda, the new king, came forward with folded hands and offered a parting word. Bana, he said, had cows in the charge of Varuna whose milk was nectar; a man who drank it became powerful and invincible in battle. Krishna's heart filled with joy at the news, and he set the errand in his mind.

The company turned homeward. Brahma blessed Krishna and departed for his own region; Indra and the storm-gods set out for Dwaraka; Usha, surrounded by her friends, started for the city of the Yadavas as well. Balarama, Krishna, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha mounted Garuda's back, and the great bird flew on, uprooting trees and shaking the earth with the beating of his wings — carrying the rescued family and a new bride toward the city that had waited for them in anxiety.
reflection: The episode rewards mercy rather than valor: the minister who counselled sparing Aniruddha receives the kingdom of the king who would not listen to him, and the war that began in a kidnapping ends in a wedding. Narada's request to hear the two families trade jests keeps the divine machinery human-sized.
next_story_tease: The journey home would end in Dwaraka, where a festival was already being readied to receive the Yadu family's newest daughter-in-law.
hero_scene: In the palace of Sonitpura, Krishna, one hand raised in assurance, confers Bana's kingdom on the folded-handed minister Kumbhanda, while behind them the wedding lights of Aniruddha and Usha blaze and the Apsaras dance.
